solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: A report that criminal finally breaks out (6)

indicatorNotes.finally: the final letter of 'criminal' is L
indicatorNotes.breaks: L breaks into BOOM, splitting it

blocks.note: a boom is a loud report, like a gunshot

annotation.surface: A news report says a convict has finally escaped from prison.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Breaks out' reads as a jailbreak, but the definition is just 'out', as flowers are out when they have opened.
annotation.definitionFit: A gardener's sense of out: blossoms that have opened fully are said to be out, in flower.

entries.clue: Country cottage phone line’s cut (5)

indicatorNotes.cut: the L for line is cut out of BLOWER

blocks.note: the blower is old British slang for the telephone

annotation.surface: The phone line to a remote country cottage has been severed.
annotation.walkthrough: 'The blower' is British slang for the phone. The 's is 'is': line is cut.
annotation.definitionFit: A bower is a shady rustic retreat, and poetically a cottage or dwelling.

entries.clue: Fuss over English conservationists obstructing channel (11)

indicatorNotes.obstructing: E and NT stand in the middle of STATION, blocking it

blocks.note: NT = the National Trust, Britain's heritage conservation charity
a TV or radio channel is a station

annotation.surface: An English conservation group causes a row by blocking a waterway.
annotation.walkthrough: The channel is a broadcasting one, not a waterway. The National Trust looks after Britain's historic houses and countryside.
annotation.definitionFit: Ostentation is showy display, a fuss made to impress.

entries.clue: Space launch low and fiery taking in both poles (8)

indicatorNotes.taking in: MOO and HOT take N and S in between them

blocks.note: to low is to moo, as cattle do
N and S, north and south poles

annotation.surface: A rocket lifts off low and blazing on a route taking it over both poles.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Low' is the cow's verb, not an adjective.
annotation.definitionFit: A moonshot is a spacecraft launched towards the Moon.

entries.clue: Work in tin and steel company (7)

blocks.note: Tata Steel, the Indian steelmaker that owns British steelworks

annotation.surface: Someone has a job in the tin and steel industry.
annotation.walkthrough: The work is a musical one, not a job.
annotation.definitionFit: A cantata is a musical work for voices and instruments.

entries.clue: Made incisive move on the dance floor? (3,2)

annotation.definition: Made incisive move on the dance floor?

blocks.note: reads as 'was sharp', but incisive comes from the Latin for cutting, so read it literally: made a cut
a ballroom manoeuvre: tapping a dancer's shoulder to take over the partner

annotation.surface: Someone made a sharp, decisive step while dancing.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Incisive' hints at cutting; on a dance floor, cutting in means tapping a dancer's shoulder to take their partner.
annotation.definitionFit: To cut in is to interrupt a dancing couple and take one partner.

entries.clue: Dander raised, wanted to strangle learner driver (7)

indicatorNotes.to strangle: NEEDED wraps round L as if throttling it

blocks.note: L = learner, from the L-plates on a learner driver's car

annotation.surface: Someone lost their temper and wanted to throttle the learner driver.
annotation.walkthrough: To get someone's dander up is to anger them. L-plates mark a British learner driver.
annotation.definitionFit: Getting someone's dander up is an old idiom for provoking anger, and being needled is being provoked by jabs.

entries.clue: Curse revolutionary crowd interrupting middle of main race (11)

indicatorNotes.revolutionary: MOB turns over to read BOM
indicatorNotes.interrupting: to interrupt is to break into the middle of something, so BOM breaks into AI
indicatorNotes.middle of: the middle of a four-letter word is its central pair, here AI from MAIN

blocks.note: the two middle letters of main
a race is a people or nation

annotation.surface: A cursing, revolutionary mob storms the course halfway through the big race.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Race' is a people, not a contest.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym in the sense of a loathsome thing or plague, as a blight is called the curse of the valley.

entries.clue: It’s served up with chicken pasty (5)

indicatorNotes.served up: in a down clue, SA is sent upwards to read AS

annotation.surface: Something is brought to the table along with a chicken pie.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pasty' looks like the Cornish pie but is the adjective for pale. 'It' as sex appeal is an old convention.
annotation.definitionFit: Both describe a sickly, colourless complexion, the grey-white of dough or of cinders.

entries.clue: Problematic rendezvous involving priest and chapter (8)

indicatorNotes.involving: to involve is to include or take in, so DATE wraps round ELI and C

blocks.note: Eli, the priest in the Book of Samuel

annotation.surface: A tricky secret meeting involves a priest and a church chapter.
annotation.walkthrough: Eli is the crossword's stock priest, from the Bible.
annotation.definitionFit: A delicate matter needs careful handling because it could easily go wrong, which makes it tricky.

entries.clue: Composer’s variable opening tied into novel (9)

indicatorNotes.opening: Z opens up the anagram and sits inside it
indicatorNotes.novel: TIED INTO is made new, rearranged

blocks.note: z is a standard algebraic variable

annotation.surface: A composer's changeable overture has been worked into a novel.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Novel' sounds like a book but is the anagram signal. Algebra's unknowns x, y and z all serve as variables.
annotation.definitionFit: Gaetano Donizetti was the Italian composer of Lucia di Lammermoor.

entries.clue: House with Contents? (5)

blocks.note: not a home but a chamber of Parliament
the capital C marks a title: members of the upper chamber vote 'Content' or 'Not content'

annotation.surface: A house is offered for sale complete with its furniture.
annotation.walkthrough: In the House of Lords, the upper chamber of the UK Parliament, members vote by saying 'Content' or 'Not content', so the Contents are those voting yes.
annotation.definitionFit: The House of Lords is the house whose voters are called Contents.

entries.clue: Method of payment in scam hardly subtle (11)

annotation.surface: A payment method is being used in a crude, obvious fraud.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface suggests card fraud, which fits the answer's world.
annotation.definitionFit: Contactless is payment by tapping a card or phone on a reader.

entries.clue: Effect of quavers on the score? (7)

annotation.definition: Effect of quavers on the score?

blocks.note: quavers look like eighth notes, but a quaver is also a tremble in the voice
a musical term written into the score for a trembling, wavering sound

annotation.surface: Someone asks how a run of short notes affects a musical score.
annotation.walkthrough: Quavers look like the eighth notes; here they are trembles in the voice, and tremolo is the trembling effect written into the score.
annotation.definitionFit: A tremolo is a rapid, wavering repetition of a note, a quavering effect.

entries.clue: By market, back in a corner, working freely (7,3,2,9)

indicatorNotes.in: HIND goes in the anagram of A CORNER
indicatorNotes.working: A CORNER is set working, rearranged

blocks.note: by = with, as in 'by means of'
an outlet is a market for goods
hind = back, as in hind legs

annotation.surface: A trader working without constraint sets up by the market, tucked away in a back corner.
annotation.walkthrough: The phrase comes from the wording of the British passport, which asks that the bearer pass 'without let or hindrance'; let is an old word for obstacle.
annotation.definitionFit: A fixed legal idiom, still printed in British passports, meaning passage allowed with no obstacle or delay.

entries.clue: Thousand initially spent on blood relative (8)

indicatorNotes.initially: the initial letter of 'spent' is S

blocks.note: a grand is a thousand pounds or dollars

annotation.surface: A thousand pounds was spent on a family member.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Thousand' as GRAND is everyday slang, and the surface's generous spending suits a grandson.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: a child's male offspring shares direct descent, so counts among kin by birth.

entries.clue: Polymath Newton entering floral decoration trade (7)

indicatorNotes.entering: to enter is to go inside, so N goes into BIZ

blocks.note: a lei is a Hawaiian garland of flowers
N is the symbol for the newton, the unit of force

annotation.surface: Isaac Newton the polymath is taking up the flower-arranging business.
annotation.walkthrough: Newton looks like Isaac, Leibniz's rival for the invention of calculus, but here it is just the unit symbol N.
annotation.definitionFit: Gottfried Leibniz was a German philosopher, mathematician and all-round polymath.

entries.clue: Caught glimpse — follow pirate (3,3)

indicatorNotes.Caught: to catch a word is to hear it, so we take the sound of 'see'

blocks.note: to dog someone is to follow them

annotation.surface: Having spotted a pirate, someone is told to go after him.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Caught' looks like the cricket C, but it is the ear catching a sound.
annotation.definitionFit: An old salt or veteran mariner; adventure stories apply the phrase to buccaneers.

entries.clue: Union to defend slave earl verbally assailed (10)

indicatorNotes.to defend: BED surrounds LABOUR and E, guarding them

blocks.note: bed stands for the marital union, as in 'bed and board'

annotation.surface: A trade union stands up for a worker and an aristocrat who were attacked with insults.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Union' looks like a trade union, and 'slave' like a noun; both mislead.
annotation.definitionFit: To belabour someone is to attack them, in words as well as blows.

entries.clue: Bats are able to develop (9)

indicatorNotes.Bats: bats means crazy, so the letters go mad

annotation.surface: Bats can grow and mature.
annotation.walkthrough: 'To' looks like it belongs to the verb 'develop', but it is the last two letters of the fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: working out a plan or argument further, adding detail and complexity.

entries.clue: Regret holding money under key in royal train? (7)

indicatorNotes.holding: RUE holds E and TIN inside it
indicatorNotes.under: in a down clue, TIN sits under E

blocks.note: tin is old British slang for money

annotation.surface: Someone on a royal train regrets keeping cash beneath a key.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Train' is not a railway: a train is the procession following a dignitary.
annotation.definitionFit: A retinue is the group of attendants following a royal, their train.

entries.clue: Something seen in some Shakespeare sonnets? (12)

annotation.definition: Something seen in some Shakespeare sonnets?

blocks.note: asks for a poetic device you can spot
three words in a row starting with S: the clue shows the device it names

annotation.surface: A literary question about a device found in a few of Shakespeare's sonnets.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue demonstrates itself: 'some Shakespeare sonnets' is a run of words beginning with the same sound.
annotation.definitionFit: Alliteration is the repetition of an initial sound across neighbouring words.

entries.clue: Shed in road, on right, and fifteenth-century house (9)

indicatorNotes.in: 'shed in road' puts the shed inside the road: CAST sits within LANE
indicatorNotes.on: in a down clue, LANE sits on top of R

blocks.note: to shed is to cast off, as a snake its skin

annotation.surface: A shed stands in the road on the right, next to an old medieval house.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Shed' looks like a garden hut but is a verb, and 'house' means a royal dynasty: Lancaster fought York in the Wars of the Roses.
annotation.definitionFit: The House of Lancaster was a royal dynasty that ruled England in the fifteenth century.

entries.clue: Cacomistle in shadow going after group (8)

indicatorNotes.going after: to go after is to follow, so TAIL is placed behind RING

blocks.note: a ring is a group, as of dealers or spies
to shadow someone is to tail them

annotation.surface: A small animal lurking in the shade trails after a group.
annotation.walkthrough: The obscure cacomistle is the definition, and the wordplay is plain.
annotation.definitionFit: The cacomistle, a raccoon relative of North America, is also called the ringtail.

entries.clue: Walsall’s second eleven on time for transport (4)

indicatorNotes.second: the second letter of Walsall is A
indicatorNotes.on: in an across clue, A and XI go on after T

blocks.note: XI is eleven in Roman numerals, and a football team

annotation.surface: Walsall's reserve football team arrive on time by coach.
annotation.walkthrough: Walsall is an English football club, so 'second eleven' reads as its reserve side; it is really the letter A plus XI.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: a hired cab carrying passengers is one kind of conveyance.

entries.clue: Greek, American and Scotsman around in those days? (8)

indicatorNotes.around: A and IAN stand either side of THEN, surrounding it

blocks.note: Ian is a typical Scottish name

annotation.surface: A Greek, an American and a Scot were together back in the day.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface sounds like the start of a joke. Ian is the crossword's stock Scotsman.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: a citizen of the Greek capital city, Athens, is one kind of Greek.

entries.clue: What gricer does for ocular irritation? (9)

blocks.note: a gricer is a railway enthusiast, who watches locomotives go by
ocular = of the eyes; tired, sore eyes

annotation.surface: A trainspotter's pastime is blamed for sore eyes.
annotation.walkthrough: A gricer is British slang for an obsessive railway enthusiast; split the answer as EYES TRAIN and it is exactly what one does.
annotation.definitionFit: Ocular means of the eyes, and staring too long at screens or print leaves them sore; a gricer spends hours watching locomotives.

entries.clue: Hint of intention corrupt union’s concealed (8)

indicatorNotes.corrupt: UNION is corrupted, its letters jumbled
indicatorNotes.concealed: the jumbled union hides END inside it

blocks.note: an end is an aim or intention

annotation.surface: A crooked trade union has hidden a hint of its real plans.
annotation.walkthrough: The 's is 'has': the union has concealed END.
annotation.definitionFit: An innuendo is an indirect hint, usually a suggestive one.

entries.clue: One periodically displaying clock not welcome in bed? (9)

annotation.definition: One periodically displaying clock not welcome in bed?

blocks.note: a plant whose fluffy seed head, shown once a year, is called a clock
the bed is a flower bed, where this plant is an unwanted weed

annotation.surface: Someone who keeps showing a clock is not wanted in the bedroom.
annotation.walkthrough: Children blow on a dandelion's seed head, called a clock, to tell the time. The bed is a flower bed, where it is an unwanted weed.
annotation.definitionFit: The dandelion is a weed whose fluffy seed head is called a clock.

entries.clue: Scrutinize bank having less adequate cover? (8)

blocks.note: a bank of seats or oars is a tier

annotation.surface: An insurer is told to check which bank offers the weaker policy.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bank' and 'cover' suggest finance and insurance; the cover is clothing, and the bank a row or tier.
annotation.definitionFit: Comparative of scanty: skimpier clothing, a thinner layer, or barely sufficient insurance all give less protection.

entries.clue: On way out: worry for operating business (5,7)

blocks.note: someone going is on the way out

annotation.surface: A business owner is anxious about a company on the verge of collapse.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a failing firm, the opposite of the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: An accounting idiom for a firm trading normally and expected to keep trading, not being wound up.

entries.clue: Mince pies and a good pint: mouthwatering (10)

indicatorNotes.Mince: to mince is to chop up, so the letters are cut up and rearranged

annotation.surface: Mince pies and a decent pint make a tempting spread.
annotation.walkthrough: Mince pies are the British Christmas pastry, but 'Mince' is the verb telling you to chop the letters.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: food that looks or smells tempting makes saliva flow and stirs hunger.

entries.clue: Supposed man-eater starts to prowl hungrily around country area (7)

indicatorNotes.starts to: the starts of 'prowl' and 'hungrily' are P and H
indicatorNotes.around: P and H stand either side of IRAN, surrounding it

blocks.note: first letters of prowl and hungrily

annotation.surface: A reputed man-eater starts to prowl hungrily around rural land.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Supposed' is fair: the piranha's man-eating reputation is largely a myth.
annotation.definitionFit: The piranha is a sharp-toothed fish reputed to eat people.

entries.clue: Crosspatch left to cork French and Spanish wines (10)

indicatorNotes.to cork: L plugs the inside of MACON, like a cork in a bottle

blocks.note: tent is an old name for Spanish red wine

annotation.surface: A grumpy person is left to cork the French and Spanish wine bottles.
annotation.walkthrough: 'French and Spanish wines' is shared: French wine is Mâcon, Spanish wine is tent, from Spanish tinto.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: a crosspatch is a grumpy, bad-tempered person, and a malcontent is chronically dissatisfied and grumbling.

entries.clue: Part from Flavian emperor endlessly breaking agreement (11)

indicatorNotes.endlessly: without an end means the last letter goes, so TITUS drops its S
indicatorNotes.breaking: to break something is to split it open, so TITU splits CONSENT

blocks.note: Titus, of the Flavian dynasty, without his last letter

annotation.surface: A section breaks away from a Flavian emperor's endless treaty.
annotation.walkthrough: The Flavians were Vespasian and his sons Titus and Domitian; only Titus fits.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: an element or ingredient making up a whole, as the constituents of a mixture.

entries.clue: Does away with Old Street main that’s shattered (12)

indicatorNotes.shattered: STREET MAIN is smashed into pieces and rebuilt

annotation.surface: Contractors rip out an old water main under the street that has burst.
annotation.walkthrough: Old Street is a real London road, which hides the EX. The anagram gives TERMINATES, itself a synonym.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: both mean destroying completely, as pest controllers wipe out vermin.

entries.clue: Specialists accepting current team for trials (11)

indicatorNotes.accepting: EXPERTS takes I and MEN inside

blocks.note: I is the symbol for electric current

annotation.surface: Specialists take on the present team for tryouts.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Current' looks like 'present'; it is the physicist's I.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: scientific tests run to discover whether a hypothesis or method holds up.

entries.clue: Old people, shuffling along with disciples, carrying a cross … (5-6)

indicatorNotes.carrying: SONS carries A and X inside

blocks.note: followers of a master are called his sons, as the sons of the prophets

annotation.surface: Elderly people shuffle along with the faithful, one carrying a cross in procession.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Old people' looks like the elderly, but means a people of long ago. The ellipsis runs the scene on into 37 down.
annotation.definitionFit: The Anglo-Saxons were the Germanic peoples who settled early medieval England.

entries.clue: Austerity perhaps for now? (8)

blocks.note: a period of austerity is a stingy, tight-fisted period
the interval until something else happens

annotation.surface: Someone wonders whether austerity is only a temporary measure.
annotation.walkthrough: Split it as MEAN TIME: a period of austerity is a stingy time. Whole, the word means the interval, as in 'for the meantime'.
annotation.definitionFit: The meantime is the present interval, as when something will do for now.

entries.clue: … observed obtrusively religious dons performing miracle? (9)

indicatorNotes.dons: PI puts on the anagram of MIRACLE like a garment, ending up inside it
indicatorNotes.performing: MIRACLE is put to work, rearranged

annotation.surface: Continuing 35 down, the pious academics are watched working a miracle.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Dons' looks like Oxford academics but is the verb for putting on clothes. PI is short for pious.
annotation.definitionFit: Empirical knowledge rests on what is observed, not theory.

entries.clue: Supposed father turning against mother? (8)

indicatorNotes.turning: PA turns round to read AP
indicatorNotes.against: against means up beside, so AP is set right next to PARENT

annotation.surface: A so-called father turns on the mother.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Supposed' opens the clue as if describing the father; it is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym in the sense of seeming true on the surface but not proven, as an apparent suicide.

entries.clue: Leaving Wagner opera, see female smile broadly? (4)

blocks.note: Lohengrin is Wagner's opera about the swan knight
lo = see, as in 'lo and behold'
a hen is a female bird

annotation.surface: Someone walks out of a Wagner opera and sees a woman beaming.
annotation.walkthrough: Leaving a four-hour Wagner opera would indeed make one smile.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: a wide beaming expression showing plenty of teeth.

entries.clue: Connected a record player I brought in one day (8)

indicatorNotes.brought in: something brought in is carried inside, so I goes inside ONE

annotation.surface: Someone hooked up a record player they brought in one day.
annotation.walkthrough: The 'record player' is not the machine but the person who plays records.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: rooms or plots that adjoin share a wall or boundary, linked side by side.

entries.clue: Paperknife artist designing text keeps exposed (6,6)

blocks.note: a letterer is an artist who designs lettering

annotation.surface: A graphic artist designing text keeps a paperknife out on the desk.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Designing' looks like an anagram signal, but the whole phrase 'artist designing text' is one word, LETTERER.
annotation.definitionFit: A paperknife is a blade for slitting envelopes, a letter opener.

entries.clue: Ultimate in espionage spy boss might authorise (7)

indicatorNotes.Ultimate in: the ultimate letter in 'espionage' is E

blocks.note: M is James Bond's boss at MI6

annotation.surface: The head of a spy agency might sign off the ultimate espionage mission.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Might' looks like a verb but is the noun, power.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: granting official permission or legal power, as a court may empower trustees to sell.

entries.clue: View from street with train (10)

blocks.note: to train a gun on something is to point it

annotation.surface: Someone watches a train pass by from the street.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Train' is the verb, as in training a camera on a target.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: the position from which someone judges things, their opinion or perspective.

entries.clue: Issue for children? (7)

blocks.note: not a problem: in wills, one's issue are one's offspring
a word that can stand in for 'children': the clue asks what kind of word that is

annotation.surface: Someone raises a problem affecting children.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Issue' looks like a problem; in wills, one's issue are one's children, so the word is a synonym for children.
annotation.definitionFit: A synonym is a word with the same meaning as another, as issue is for children.

entries.clue: Carrying foie gras, maybe ship floods (6)

blocks.note: foie gras is one kind of pâté

annotation.surface: A ship carrying a cargo of foie gras may be swamped.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Maybe' marks foie gras as an example of pâté. 'Floods' is a noun here, not a verb.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: a river in spate has risen suddenly after heavy rain and overflows.

entries.clue: Scullers at the outset row hard (5)

blocks.note: a row is a quarrel, a tiff

annotation.surface: Rowers set off by pulling hard on their oars.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Row' rhymes with cow here: an argument, not rowing a boat.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym in the sense of difficult or demanding, as a stiff climb, exam or penalty.

entries.clue: Military group must shed tons for diet (7)

indicatorNotes.must shed: to shed is to lose or cast off, so REGIMENT loses its T

blocks.note: a regiment is a military unit

annotation.surface: An overweight army unit needs to lose tons by dieting.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface's weight-loss joke is exactly the mechanism.
annotation.definitionFit: A regimen is a prescribed course of diet or exercise.

entries.clue: Clergyman’s land bishop fenced with joy (5)

indicatorNotes.fenced with: a fence encloses a field, so GLEE encloses B

annotation.surface: A bishop happily puts a fence around a vicar's field.
annotation.walkthrough: Glebe is church land farmed to support the parish priest, a British term.
annotation.definitionFit: Glebe is land assigned to a clergyman as part of his living.

entries.clue: A scruffy old bear inspiring great affection (8)

indicatorNotes.scruffy: OLD BEAR is made scruffy, messed up

annotation.surface: A tatty old teddy bear is still dearly loved.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a child's worn teddy, which is exactly what the answer describes.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: cute, lovable things such as kittens and teddies make people dote on them.

entries.clue: City wife in Nasa rockets? (5)

indicatorNotes.in: W goes in the anagram of NASA
indicatorNotes.rockets: NASA is sent rocketing, its letters scrambled

annotation.surface: An astronaut's wife asks whether a city is going up in Nasa rockets.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Rockets' looks like spacecraft but is a verb: the letters of NASA shoot about.
annotation.definitionFit: Aswan is a city in southern Egypt, by the Aswan Dam.

entries.clue: Young female duck or cattle catcher? (5)

blocks.note: a duck is a score of nothing in cricket, 0

annotation.surface: A quiz asks whether something is a young female duck or a device for catching cattle.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Young female duck' reads as a duckling, but the duck is cricket's zero, O.
annotation.definitionFit: A lasso is a looped rope for catching cattle.

entries.clue: Song as yours truly makes the house lights come up? (4,2,8,7)

annotation.definition: Song as yours truly makes the house lights come up?

blocks.note: a song title spoken in the first person: yours truly is me

blocks.clueFragment: makes the house lights come up?
blocks.note: not theatre lighting: a house's lights are its panes of glass, which come up bright when washed

annotation.surface: A performer sings as the theatre lights go up at the end of the show.
annotation.walkthrough: 'When I'm Cleaning Windows' is George Formby's 1936 comic song. 'Yours truly' is me, and a house's lights are its windows, which come up bright when cleaned.
annotation.definitionFit: It is a famous song by the British comedian George Formby about a window cleaner.

entries.clue: Obliged to pull back, about to assess force (8)

indicatorNotes.back: LUG is pulled back to read GUL
indicatorNotes.about: GUL goes about RATE and F

blocks.note: to lug is to pull or drag

annotation.surface: Someone forced to retreat is about to weigh up their strength.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Obliged' reads as 'forced', but it is the thankful sense: much obliged.
annotation.definitionFit: The thankful sense, as in the polite phrase 'much obliged', meaning thanks for a favour received.

entries.clue: Photography pioneer’s direction to staff (7)

blocks.note: to staff a post is to man it

annotation.surface: A photography pioneer issues an instruction to his employees.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Direction' looks like an order to the staff; it is a compass point, and 'staff' is the verb.
annotation.definitionFit: George Eastman founded Kodak and popularised roll film.

entries.clue: What acne treatment promises to do for tyrant? (6)

annotation.definition2: What acne treatment promises to do

blocks.clueFragment: What acne treatment promises to do
blocks.note: a spot cream promises to rid the skin of pimples
a tyrant is an absolute ruler

annotation.surface: Someone asks what a spot cream claims to do for a dictator.
annotation.walkthrough: Split the answer as DE-SPOT for the joke: to remove spots.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym for an absolute ruler wielding cruel power; split DE-SPOT it becomes what a pimple cream claims.
